children: By Kimberley Kao
Indian equities have been one of the world's worst performers so far this year, but that hasn't shaken billionaire investor Raamdeo Agrawal's faith in the market.
The chairman of Mumbai-based firm Motilal Oswal Financial Services, which manages about $70 billion in assets, says he is "fully invested" in India.
Calling India the "ultimate bullish market," Agrawal expects the stock market to double from current levels within the next five to six years.
India hasn't done well over the last two years, but that doesn't mean the story has changed, he said. "India is a secular story, not a one-off."
Agrawal's position of investing solely in Indian stands in contrast to that of foreign institutional investors.

Many investors have soured on India with the Middle East conflict pushing up energy prices, raising economic risks, pressuring capital flows and hurting the oil-sensitive rupee. Concerns about valuations and the lack of an artificial-intelligence story have contributed to the flight of foreign capital.
Foreign ownership in Indian equities hit a 15-year low in June, according to data from Goldman Sachs.
India's benchmark Sensex index has shed over 10% this year as other Asian markets boom thanks to AI. South Korea's Kospi is up about 67% and Taiwan's Taiex has gained 64%.
As investors rotate toward AI, MSCI has raised allocations for Taiwanese and South Korean equities in its Emerging Market Index.
India's weighting is now roughly 11%, compared with about 20% in 2024, Agrawal noted.
But he's unfazed. He thinks sentiment will brighten and that the foreign institutional selloff has likely bottomed out.

That's a view echoed by Goldman Sachs analysts who wrote in a recent note that foreign selling is likely over. Fears of an economic slowdown hurt stock valuations in the first half of the year but sentiment should turn favorable thanks to an improved domestic outlook and ultra-light foreign positioning, GS said.

Recent data backs that up: India's economy in the April-June quarter grew a solid 7.8% compared with the same period a year earlier, despite the Middle East energy shock. India's National Securities Depository data show that foreign institutional inflows touched a near two-year high in August.
Agrawal sees scope for India's economy to keep growing at a 7% to 8% clip over the next two to three decades.
"U.S. tariffs and crude oil prices are now the only headwinds...I believe both of them will get sorted in the near future," he said.
A robust pipeline of initial public offerings, including SBI Funds Management's $1 billion listing in July, signals that capital market activity is accelerating.
Money from retail investors has also been flowing into mutual funds as the emergence of various digital financial platforms makes investing easier, Agrawal said.
The investor, who has a personal net worth of about $2.4 billion, says his strategy is anchored in quality growth stocks.
"I never had any cash ever in my portfolio," he said. "I'm fully invested and I love to sell or buy things."
So where is he putting his money? In equity instruments like Motilal Oswal Equity Mutual Funds and Motilal Oswal private-equity funds, as well as direct stocks managed by the company.
By sector, he thinks India's quick commerce industry could produce quarter-trillion-dollar companies over the next decade.
There's value in India IT and software too, despite a bruising selloff sparked by the rollout of AI-powered services that can replace people.
That reaction is overdone, Agrawal said, adding that the view of India as an "anti-AI story" is misplaced.
Indian IT services providers can ride the AI wave to become the primary deployers of AI software for sectors like banking, he said.
"We are the biggest [AI] user in the world..So all the implementation for every country, every company, will [eventually] be done by Indians."
